blocks.text: A wing-root fitting on a transport aircraft carries the same load whether it is made of steel, aluminium or titanium, but a kilogram saved on every fitting is a kilogram of fuel or payload saved on every flight. The choice of alloy family is therefore driven by strength per unit mass, not strength alone.

blocks.markdown: Steels, aluminium alloys and titanium alloys all deform by dislocation slip, but they differ in density, in how they are strengthened and in what else they offer: conductivity, corrosion behaviour, cost and ease of fabrication. In this unit we compare the three families on **specific strength**, see how an aluminium-copper alloy is hardened by precipitates, and then use the comparison to choose a family for three real components.

blocks.title: Specific strength
blocks.text: Specific strength is the yield strength divided by density, $\sigma_y/\rho$, with $\sigma_y$ in Pa and $\rho$ in kg m$^{-3}$, giving N m kg$^{-1}$. It measures how much stress a unit mass of material can sustain, so it governs the mass of tension-loaded parts.

blocks.latex: \text{specific strength}=\frac{\sigma_y}{\rho}\qquad m=\rho A L=\frac{\rho F L}{\sigma_{\mathrm{allow}}}
blocks.caption: For a tie of length L carrying force F, the required area is A = F/sigma_allow, so mass is proportional to rho/sigma_allow, the reciprocal of specific strength.

blocks.title: Comparing specific strength
blocks.prompt: Using the typical values $\sigma_y=1000$ MPa, $\rho=7850$ kg m$^{-3}$ for a quenched and tempered alloy steel; $\sigma_y=500$ MPa, $\rho=2810$ kg m$^{-3}$ for aluminium 7075-T6; and $\sigma_y=880$ MPa, $\rho=4430$ kg m$^{-3}$ for Ti-6Al-4V, rank the three by specific strength.

steps.text: Write the ratio for each alloy and keep SI units (1 MPa = $10^{6}$ Pa).
Steel: divide the yield strength by the density.
Rank: titanium is highest, aluminium second, steel lowest, even though the steel has the highest yield strength in absolute terms.

blocks.answer: Ti-6Al-4V about 199 kN m/kg, then 7075-T6 about 178 kN m/kg, then alloy steel about 127 kN m/kg (typical values).

rows: Highest absolute strength, heavy, needs corrosion protection
Good corrosion resistance and weldable; formed in the O or T4 condition, with T6 used for strength
Excellent corrosion resistance, keeps strength to about 300 C, costly
blocks.caption: Typical room-temperature values; real values depend on temper and product form.

blocks.markdown: **Stiffness is a different story.** The elastic moduli of steel, titanium and aluminium are about 210, 110 to 115 and 70 GPa (typical; 110 is used here for titanium), so $E/\rho$ is about 26.8, 24.8 and 25.9 GPa per Mg m$^{-3}$: nearly the same. Swapping steel for aluminium therefore does not make a stiffness-limited part lighter by itself; the saving comes from using a thicker, more efficient section.

**Precipitation hardening of Al-Cu.** Pure aluminium is soft (yield about 20 to 30 MPa) and the strengthening of most aerospace aluminium alloys comes from fine precipitates. In an alloy such as Al-4.5 wt% Cu, copper dissolves in aluminium at high temperature (up to about 5.7 wt% at 548 C, typical) but only about 0.2 wt% at room temperature. The three-step route exploits that falling solubility.

items: **Solution treat** at about 500 C: all Cu dissolves, giving one homogeneous $\alpha$ solid solution.
**Quench** rapidly in water: Cu has no time to leave solution, so the alloy is a *supersaturated* solid solution, soft and ductile.

**Age** at room temperature (natural) or about 130 to 190 C (artificial): Cu atoms cluster into Guinier-Preston zones, then coherent $\theta''$ and semi-coherent $\theta'$ plates, finally equilibrium incoherent $\theta$ (CuAl$_2$, about 54 wt% Cu).

blocks.markdown: The fine, closely spaced coherent precipitates distort the lattice and must be sheared or bypassed by moving dislocations, which raises the stress needed for slip. Hardness peaks when the precipitates are very small and dense. If ageing is continued or the temperature is too high, the precipitates coarsen and become incoherent, the spacing between them grows, dislocations bow between them easily, and the alloy softens: this is **overageing**.

blocks.title: Amount of precipitate in an aged Al-Cu alloy
blocks.prompt: An Al-4.5 wt% Cu alloy is fully aged and has reached equilibrium at room temperature. Take the $\alpha$ phase to contain 0.2 wt% Cu and the precipitate $\theta$ (CuAl$_2$) to contain 54 wt% Cu (typical). What mass fraction of the alloy is $\theta$?

steps.text: Use the lever rule on the tie line between the two phase compositions: the fraction of $\theta$ is the distance from the alloy to the $\alpha$ end divided by the tie-line length.
Insert the compositions in wt% Cu.

blocks.answer: About 8 wt% of the alloy is the precipitate phase and 92 wt% is the aluminium-rich matrix.

blocks.markdown: **Titanium and copper.** Titanium alloys have a stable surface oxide giving outstanding corrosion resistance and good strength to about 300 C, but they are expensive and have poor thermal conductivity (about 7 W m$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$, typical). Copper alloys combine high electrical conductivity (pure copper near 100 % IACS, about $5.8\times10^{7}$ S m$^{-1}$) and thermal conductivity (about 390 W m$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$, typical) with good water and seawater corrosion resistance. Alloying raises strength but lowers conductivity. Steady conduction through a thin flat wall of thickness $t$ gives heat flux $q=k\,\Delta T/t$.

rows: Highest specific strength; titanium if temperature or corrosion is severe
High thermal conductivity with good corrosion and biofouling resistance
Conductivity plus enough strength and elastic spring
blocks.caption: Matching the dominant requirement to an alloy family.

blocks.title: Absolute strength is not specific strength
blocks.text: A steel with the highest yield strength can still lose on strength per mass, and a lighter alloy is only better if the part is limited by strength or stiffness per mass. Always check the dominant constraint (strength, stiffness, conductivity, corrosion, cost) before ranking.

points: Specific strength $\sigma_y/\rho$ ranks Ti-6Al-4V above 7075-T6 above alloy steel (typical values), though steel is strongest in absolute terms.

Al-Cu hardens by solution treating, quenching to a supersaturated solid solution, then ageing to form fine coherent precipitates that obstruct dislocations; overageing coarsens them and softens the alloy.
Choose by the dominant requirement: titanium or 7xxx aluminium for light structure, copper alloys for heat exchangers and electrical contacts.

questions.stem: Four candidate alloys are listed with typical room-temperature data. Which has the highest specific strength?

options.text: A steel with $\sigma_y=1200$ MPa and $\rho=7850$ kg m$^{-3}$
An aluminium alloy with $\sigma_y=300$ MPa and $\rho=2700$ kg m$^{-3}$
A titanium alloy with $\sigma_y=900$ MPa and $\rho=4500$ kg m$^{-3}$
A copper alloy with $\sigma_y=400$ MPa and $\rho=8900$ kg m$^{-3}$

questions.correctOptionText: A titanium alloy with $\sigma_y=900$ MPa and $\rho=4500$ kg m$^{-3}$

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: it has the greatest yield strength but 1200/7850 is only 153 kN m/kg.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: 300/2700 is only 111 kN m/kg; low density does not compensate for low strength.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: 900/4500 gives 200 kN m/kg, the largest of the four.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: 400/8900 is only 45 kN m/kg because of the high density.

questions.explanation: Specific strength is $\sigma_y/\rho$: the titanium alloy gives $900\times10^{6}/4500=2.0\times10^{5}$ N m/kg, the steel 153 kN m/kg, the aluminium 111 kN m/kg and the copper alloy 45 kN m/kg. The ranking differs from the ranking by yield strength alone, because density matters for mass-limited design.

questions.stem: A tie rod must carry a tensile load of 15 kN. Design the allowable stress as $0.6\sigma_y$. For an aluminium alloy with $\sigma_y=480$ MPa and $\rho=2800$ kg m$^{-3}$, find the mass of one metre of rod, in kg per metre.
questions.explanation: The allowable stress is $0.6\times480=288$ MPa, so the required area is $A=15000/(288\times10^{6})=5.21\times10^{-5}$ m$^2$. The mass per metre is $\rho A=2800\times5.21\times10^{-5}=0.146$ kg/m.

questions.stem: Why does a freshly quenched Al-4.5 wt% Cu alloy become much harder after being aged at 150 C?

options.text: Fine coherent copper-rich precipitates form and obstruct the motion of dislocations
The quench converts the aluminium to a body-centred cubic structure that is inherently stronger
Ageing removes the dissolved copper so the matrix becomes pure and therefore harder
Ageing introduces a high density of vacancies that lock the grain boundaries

questions.correctOptionText: Fine coherent copper-rich precipitates form and obstruct the motion of dislocations

distractorRationale.a: Correct: precipitate clusters and plates form from the supersaturated solution and impede slip.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: aluminium stays face-centred cubic throughout; no structural change causes the hardening.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: pure aluminium is very soft, and the matrix is not hardened by removing solute; it is the precipitates that harden.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: vacancies assist diffusion in the early stage but do not harden by locking grain boundaries.

questions.explanation: The quench traps copper in a supersaturated solid solution; heating at 150 C lets copper atoms diffuse into Guinier-Preston zones and $\theta''$ and $\theta'$ precipitates. These coherent particles must be cut or bypassed by dislocations, so the yield strength rises.

questions.stem: An Al-Cu alloy is held for a very long time at 300 C after solution treatment and quenching, and its hardness falls below its peak value. What microstructural change explains this?

options.text: All of the precipitates redissolve and the alloy returns to the soft supersaturated state
The matrix recrystallises into a single grain that has no precipitates at all
The aluminium oxidises internally and the oxide particles are weaker than the matrix
The precipitates coarsen and become widely spaced and incoherent, so dislocations bypass them easily

questions.correctOptionText: The precipitates coarsen and become widely spaced and incoherent, so dislocations bypass them easily

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: at 300 C the precipitates dissolve only partly, and full redissolution would need a temperature near the solvus; the softening is due to coarsening.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: recrystallisation is a cold-work phenomenon and is not the cause of overageing.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: no internal oxidation is involved in heat treatment of Al-Cu in normal atmospheres.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: overageing coarsens the precipitates, increases their spacing and loses coherency.

questions.explanation: Hardness is greatest when precipitates are small, dense and coherent. At long times or high temperature, larger particles grow at the expense of smaller ones, the inter-particle spacing grows, and dislocations bow between particles at lower stress, so the alloy overages and softens.

questions.stem: An Al-4.5 wt% Cu alloy has reached equilibrium at room temperature, with the aluminium-rich matrix containing 0.2 wt% Cu and the CuAl$_2$ precipitate containing 54 wt% Cu. Find the mass percentage of the alloy that is CuAl$_2$ using the lever rule, in per cent. (Use these values, not any table.)
questions.explanation: The lever rule gives $f=(C_0-C_\alpha)/(C_\theta-C_\alpha)=(4.5-0.2)/(54-0.2)$. This is $4.3/53.8=0.080$, so 8.0 % of the alloy is precipitate.

questions.stem: Which alloy family is the most suitable for a spring electrical contact that must conduct current and remain elastic through many cycles of insertion?

options.text: Ti-6Al-4V, because it has the best specific strength
A beryllium-copper or phosphor-bronze alloy
A 7075-T6 aluminium alloy, because it is light and strong
A quenched and tempered alloy steel, because it has the highest yield strength

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: titanium has low electrical conductivity and its specific strength is irrelevant to a contact.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: copper alloys combine high electrical conductivity with enough strength and elastic range for spring contacts.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: aluminium conducts well but has a lower yield strength than needed and forms a high-resistance oxide film at the contact surface.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: steel is a poor electrical conductor and corrodes, raising contact resistance.

questions.explanation: A connector needs electrical conductivity first and then spring strength. Copper alloys such as phosphor bronze and beryllium copper keep a good fraction of the conductivity of copper while being strengthened by solid solution, cold work or precipitation, whereas titanium and steel conduct poorly.

questions.stem: A condenser tube wall is made of a copper alloy of thermal conductivity 385 W m$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$ (typical) and thickness 1.2 mm. The temperature difference across the wall is 8 K. Assuming one-dimensional steady conduction through a flat wall, find the heat flux in MW m$^{-2}$.
questions.explanation: Steady conduction gives $q=k\Delta T/t=385\times8/0.0012=2.57\times10^{6}$ W m$^{-2}$. This is 2.57 MW m$^{-2}$, about 55 times larger than for a titanium wall of the same size with $k\approx7$ W m$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$, which is why copper alloys are preferred for heat exchangers.

questions.stem: A designer proposes replacing a steel beam with an aluminium alloy beam of identical cross-section, expecting a lighter beam of similar stiffness. Using typical values $E_{\mathrm{steel}}=210$ GPa, $\rho_{\mathrm{steel}}=7850$ kg m$^{-3}$, $E_{\mathrm{Al}}=70$ GPa and $\rho_{\mathrm{Al}}=2700$ kg m$^{-3}$, what is the main problem?

options.text: The aluminium beam is stiffer, because its density is lower
The aluminium beam has the same stiffness, because stiffness depends only on cross-section shape
The aluminium beam has higher stiffness per mass only if it is aged, as ageing raises the modulus
The aluminium beam has about one third of the stiffness, because $E/\rho$ of the two metals is similar, so the section must be enlarged

questions.correctOptionText: The aluminium beam has about one third of the stiffness, because $E/\rho$ of the two metals is similar, so the section must be enlarged

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: lower density does not raise the modulus; a lighter beam of the same section is less stiff.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: stiffness depends on the modulus times the second moment of area, not on the shape alone.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: heat treatment changes strength but barely changes the elastic modulus.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: with the same section, deflection is inversely proportional to $E$, so the aluminium beam deflects three times more; the weight saving appears only with a larger section, because $E/\rho$ is about 26.8 versus 25.9 GPa per Mg m$^{-3}$.

questions.explanation: Beam stiffness is proportional to $EI$, so with identical $I$ the aluminium beam is 70/210, one third, as stiff. Specific stiffness $E/\rho$ is nearly the same for steel and aluminium, so equal-stiffness aluminium beams are lighter only in so far as the section is made deeper to raise $I$.

questions.stem: A designer must select an alloy family for (i) an aircraft seat-rail bracket, (ii) a seawater-cooled heat-exchanger tube and (iii) an electrical connector pin. Select a family for each and justify the choice using the dominant requirement.
markingGuide: (i) Bracket: titanium (e.g. Ti-6Al-4V) or high-strength 7xxx aluminium chosen for high specific strength; may mention titanium when corrosion or temperature is severe
(i) States that mass saving is the driver, so $\sigma_y/\rho$ is the criterion
(ii) Tube: copper alloy (brass or cupronickel) or possibly titanium; justified by high thermal conductivity and seawater corrosion resistance
(iii) Connector: copper alloy (phosphor bronze or beryllium copper) justified by electrical conductivity and spring strength
Rejects an unsuitable alternative with a reason (for example titanium for conductors because of low conductivity)
questions.explanation: Each component is dominated by a different requirement: mass for the bracket, heat flow plus corrosion for the tube, and conductivity plus spring strength for the connector. A good answer names the dominant requirement first and then the family that supplies it.

questions.stem: Explain how precipitation hardening strengthens an Al-Cu alloy. Describe the three stages of the heat treatment, and explain why continued ageing at high temperature reduces strength.
markingGuide: Solution treatment dissolves Cu into a single-phase solid solution at high temperature
Quench traps Cu in a supersaturated solid solution, giving a soft, ductile alloy
Ageing precipitates fine coherent particles (Guinier-Preston zones, $\theta''$, $\theta'$) from the supersaturated solution
Dislocations must cut or bypass these particles, raising the yield strength
Overageing: precipitates coarsen and become incoherent and widely spaced, dislocations bypass easily and strength falls
questions.explanation: The strengthening depends on a fine, dense dispersion of obstacles formed from the supersaturated solution. Coarsening reduces the number of obstacles and increases their spacing, so the stress to move dislocations falls again.
